planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs after the last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; this smooth-leaved variety was introduced to Florida nurseries from a South African botanical garden in the 1980s and is frequently mislabeled 'native' firebush, so confirm the variety before planting in a wildlife or native-restoration bed.

directions: Hamelia patens var. glabra is the smooth-leaved, tropical American and South American variety of firebush that entered the Florida nursery trade decades ago under the misleading name African Firebush and is still widely sold that way, in contrast to the rough-textured, Florida-native var. patens. The two varieties look similar at a glance, but this one has glossier, less hairy foliage and flowers that trend more orange-yellow than the fiery red-orange of the native form, and it lacks the same depth of documented wildlife value. It blooms in dense terminal clusters from late spring through fall and still draws hummingbirds and butterflies reliably, making it a serviceable ornamental where the true native is unavailable. Because it can cross-pollinate with native firebush and dilute the wild gene pool, gardeners working near natural areas or restoration sites should seek out var. patens instead. Give it full sun, lean well-drained soil, and expect the same root-hardy dieback-and-resprout pattern after hard freezes as the native variety.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Gardening Solutions: Firebush
Florida Association of Native Nurseries — The Hamelia Mess

planting.note: Set out container plants in spring in full sun with lean, well-drained soil; var. angustata is the narrow-leaved Chihuahuan Desert form of yellow bells and is markedly more cold-tolerant than tropical Tecoma stans selections, holding foliage into the mid-20s F and resprouting reliably after freezes into the low teens.

directions: Tecoma stans var. angustata is a narrow-leaflet, naturally more compact and cold-hardy variety of yellow bells native to the Chihuahuan Desert region, distinguished from typical tropical T. stans by its finer-textured foliage and superior tolerance of hard freezes. It flowers on current-season growth, producing the same clusters of golden-yellow trumpet blooms from summer through fall, so any winter dieback is simply pruned away in early spring without sacrificing that year's bloom. Establishment is easiest in lean, fast-draining soil and full sun, where it becomes strongly drought tolerant and needs little supplemental water once its roots are established. Hummingbirds and long-tongued native bees use the tubular flowers heavily through the warm months. For gardeners at the cooler edge of yellow bells' range — zone 7b-8 — this variety is the most reliable choice among all Tecoma stans forms for surviving winter without a full replant.
sources: Civano Nursery — Yellow Bells, Tecoma stans var. angustata
Water Use It Wisely (Arizona Municipal Water Users Association) — Yellow Bells, Orange Bells & More
Whitfill Nursery — Tecoma stans angustata, Arizona Yellow Bells

common_name: Sierra Apricot Tecoma (Compact Coral-Apricot Hybrid Esperanza)

planting.note: Set out container plants after the last frost in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, lean soil; Sierra Apricot (patented as 'Mnstapbe') is a Mountain States Wholesale Nursery introduction bred for a low, dense, seed-free habit that stays in nearly continuous bloom rather than cycling on and off between flower flushes.

directions: Sierra Apricot is a compact hybrid tecoma bred specifically for size and bloom persistence — at 2-3 feet tall and wider than tall, it stays proportionate to small residential beds and large containers where standard esperanza would quickly outgrow the space. Its trumpet-shaped flowers open a warm coral-apricot rather than the golden yellow of straight-species Tecoma stans, and because the cultivar sets very little seed, energy that would go into seedpods instead fuels a longer, denser bloom cycle from spring through fall. Plant it in full sun and lean, well-drained soil; it is highly heat and drought tolerant once established and is well suited to xeric borders alongside agave, salvia, and other low-water Gulf South or Southwest plantings. In zone 8, expect a hard freeze to kill the plant to the ground, but it resprouts vigorously from the base and returns to bloom by midsummer.
sources: Mountain States Wholesale Nursery — Tecoma x Sierra Apricot
Devil Mountain Wholesale Nursery — Tecoma 'Sierra Apricot'
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tecoma in Southern Gardens

common_name: Crimson Flare Tecoma (Large Red-Flowered Hybrid Esperanza)

planting.note: Set out container plants after the last frost in full sun, including reflected-heat sites, in well-drained soil; Crimson Flare is a fast-growing Mountain States Wholesale Nursery hybrid that reaches small-tree proportions and benefits from a hard pruning in late winter to keep it shrub-form and densely flowering.

directions: Crimson Flare is a vigorous hybrid tecoma selected for large clusters of red to orange-red trumpet flowers that often soften toward pink as summer heat intensifies, a striking departure from the clear yellow of straight-species esperanza. Deep green, glossy foliage sets off the bloom color and holds up well through the heat and reflected sun of a west-facing wall or paved courtyard, sites where many other flowering shrubs scorch. It grows quickly to a full 8 feet tall and wide, so it reads more as a small flowering tree or informal hedge than a compact border plant, and an annual late-winter pruning keeps growth dense and encourages the heaviest flowering. It is highly drought and heat tolerant once established and draws hummingbirds steadily from spring through fall. In zone 8, expect dieback to the ground after a hard freeze, with vigorous resprouting from the base and a return to bloom by midsummer.
sources: Mountain States Wholesale Nursery — Tecoma x Crimson Flare
Devil Mountain Wholesale Nursery — Tecoma x Crimson Flare
